title: Extra Information: Commas, Dashes and Brackets in Pairs
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Grammar: Boundaries
summary: Essential vs extra information: the removal test, matching pairs, appositives, names and titles, and which / that / who clauses — with 10 practice questions.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Extra-information questions are part of the **Boundaries** skill in the **Standard English Conventions** domain (about 26% of the scored Reading and Writing questions, 11–15 questions in total). The College Board lists **supplements** — appositives and parenthetical elements — as one of the things this skill checks, together with knowing when **no punctuation** is needed.

You see one short passage (25–150 words) with a blank and the question **“Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?”** The four choices usually have the same words with commas, dashes or brackets in different places — or no punctuation at all. To answer, you must decide two things: (1) is this piece of information **essential** or **extra**? and (2) if it is extra, where does it **start** and where does it **end**?

blocks.title: الفكرة كلها في سؤالين
blocks.text: اسأل نفسك: لو شلت الكلام ده، الجملة تفضل صح ومعناها الأساسي ما يتغيرش؟ لو آه، يبقى معلومة إضافية ولازم تتحط بين علامتين متشابهتين: فاصلة…فاصلة أو شرطة…شرطة أو قوس…قوس. لو المعنى اتغير أو بقى مش واضح، يبقى معلومة أساسية ومن غير أي علامات.
Rule 1: The removal test — essential or extra?

**Extra (non-essential) information** adds a detail, but the sentence is still complete and keeps its main meaning without it. It is set off with punctuation. **Essential information** tells us *which one* we mean; without it the meaning changes or becomes unclear. Essential information takes **no** punctuation.

items: Find the words that might be extra (a description, a name, a which/who clause, a phrase starting with a past participle).
Cover them with your finger and read the rest of the sentence.
Still complete AND still the same main meaning → **extra** → a matching pair of marks around it.
The sentence breaks, or now means something different or unclear → **essential** → no marks.

rows: My grandfather, a retired engineer, still repairs radios.
“My grandfather still repairs radios.” Same meaning.
Extra → commas ✓
Students who finish early may leave.
“Students may leave.” Now ALL students may leave — meaning changed.
Essential → no commas ✓
The Nile, which flows north, ends in the Mediterranean.
“The Nile ends in the Mediterranean.” Still clear — there is only one Nile.
Extra → commas ✓
The phone that I bought yesterday is broken.
“The phone is broken.” Which phone? Unclear.
Essential → no commas ✓
The bridge, built in 1902, is still used today.
“The bridge is still used today.” Clear if the text has only one bridge.
Extra → commas ✓
Of the two bridges, the bridge built in 1902 is older.
“Of the two bridges, the bridge is older.” Which one? Nonsense.
Essential → no commas ✓

blocks.title: The context decides
blocks.text: The same words can be essential in one passage and extra in another. “The bridge built in 1902” needs no commas if the passage talks about two bridges, but takes commas if there is only one. Always read the sentence before the blank: it often tells you whether there is one thing or many.
Rule 2: Matching pairs — comma…comma, dash…dash, bracket…bracket

Extra information in the **middle** of a sentence needs a mark on **both** sides, and the two marks must **match**. Commas, dashes and brackets are all correct; you may not open with one and close with another.

items: ✓ The festival, held every spring, attracts thousands of visitors.
✓ The festival—held every spring—attracts thousands of visitors.
✓ The festival (held every spring) attracts thousands of visitors.
✗ The festival, held every spring—attracts thousands of visitors. (comma … dash)
✗ The festival—held every spring, attracts thousands of visitors. (dash … comma)
✗ The festival (held every spring, attracts thousands of visitors. (bracket never closed)
✗ The festival, held every spring attracts thousands of visitors. (pair not closed — now one comma splits the subject from its verb)
✗ The festival held every spring, attracts thousands of visitors. (pair not opened)

blocks.text: If the extra information comes at the **end** of the sentence, you need only the opening mark; the period closes it: “The prize went to Hana Fouad, a young engineer from Aswan.” If it comes at the very **start**, you need only the closing mark: “A retired engineer, my grandfather still repairs radios.”

**Which mark should you choose?** All three are correct, so the test will not ask you to choose between a correct pair of commas and a correct pair of dashes. The question is always: which mark did the writer **already** use? Dashes are especially useful when the extra information itself contains commas: “The three winners—Hana, Omar, and Rana—received medals.”

blocks.title: Look back for the first mark
blocks.text: When the blank comes right after some extra information, look back to where that information began. A comma, a dash or a bracket there tells you exactly which mark must close it. When the blank comes at the start of the extra information, look forward for the closing mark.
Rule 3: Appositives — a noun that renames a noun

An **appositive** is a noun phrase placed next to another noun to rename or describe it: “Naguib Mahfouz, **a Nobel Prize winner**, was born in Cairo.” Most appositives are extra and take a matching pair. But an appositive can also be **essential**, when it tells us which one of several things we mean.

rows: Aswan, a city on the Nile, is famous for its granite.
There is one Aswan; the description is extra.
Pair of commas ✓
Mahfouz's novel Palace Walk was published in 1956.
Mahfouz wrote many novels; the title tells us which one.
No commas ✓
Mahfouz's last novel, Qushtumur, was published in 1988.
A writer has only one last novel; the title is extra.
Pair of commas ✓
My friend Omar lent me his calculator.
I have many friends; the name says which one.
No commas ✓
My oldest friend, Omar, lent me his calculator.
Only one person can be my oldest friend.
Pair of commas ✓

items: ✗ Aswan a city on the Nile, is famous for its granite. (opening comma missing)
✗ Mahfouz's novel, Palace Walk, was published in 1956. (commas suggest he wrote only one novel)

blocks.text: Rule 4: Names and titles — “the biologist Maria Lopez” vs “the biologist, Maria Lopez,”
This is one of the most tested comma rules on the SAT, because your ear wants a pause that grammar does not allow. Ask: **does the label before the name already point to one single person?**

rows: Job title or label directly before a name, no “the” or “a”
No commas
✓ Biologist Maria Lopez studied the reef. / ✓ Egyptian author Naguib Mahfouz …
“the” + general label + name (many people have that job)
No commas — the name is essential
✓ The biologist Maria Lopez studied the reef.
A description that fits only one person + name
Pair of commas — the name is extra
✓ The team's only biologist, Maria Lopez, studied the reef.
Name first, then the description
Pair of commas around the description
✓ Maria Lopez, a biologist, studied the reef.
Only one comma between label and name, or after the name
✗ Never
✗ Biologist, Maria Lopez studied … / ✗ The biologist Maria Lopez, studied …

blocks.text: Words that make a description unique: **only, first, last, oldest, current, the director of, the founder of, her husband, his mother**. Words such as **an, one of, a famous, the Egyptian** usually mean the label is general, so the name is essential.

items: ✓ The museum's director, Amal Saad, opened the exhibition. (a museum has one director)
✓ Director Amal Saad opened the exhibition. (title before name)
✓ One of the curators, Samy Fathy, gave the tour. (the name is extra after a complete description)
✗ The curator, Samy Fathy gave the tour. (pair not closed — comma between subject and verb)

blocks.title: The label + name trap
blocks.text: Choices such as “author, Ahmed Khaled” or “painter Laila Said,” look natural but are wrong. A label directly before a name takes no comma, and a comma after the name with no partner before it splits the subject from its verb.
Rule 5: Relative clauses — which, that, who, whose, where

rows: which
Extra information about things
Comma before it (and after the clause if the sentence continues)
✓ The Cairo Metro, which opened in 1987, carries millions of passengers.
that
Essential information about things
Never a comma before “that”
✓ The line that runs to Helwan is the oldest.
who
People — essential or extra
Commas only when extra
✓ Students who study daily improve fastest. / ✓ Dr. Nadia Samir, who leads the project, …
whose / where
Essential or extra
Same removal test
✓ Siwa, where olives grow well, is far from Cairo. / ✓ The town where I grew up is small.

items: ✗ The line, that runs to Helwan, is the oldest. (“that” never takes commas on the test)
✗ The Cairo Metro which opened in 1987, carries millions of passengers. (pair not opened)
✓ After a person's name, a who-clause is almost always extra, because the name already tells us who: “Dr. Nadia Samir, who leads the project, …”
✗ Students, who study daily, improve fastest. (now it says ALL students study daily)

blocks.text: Rule 6: Interrupters and participle phrases

Short phrases that interrupt a clause are also extra information and need a matching pair: **however, for example, in fact, of course, according to the report, as a result**. Phrases that begin with a past participle (built, held, known, written) or an -ing word follow the removal test too.

items: ✓ The final results, however, were different.
✗ The final results, however were different. (pair not closed)
✓ The survey, according to its authors, is the largest of its kind.
✓ The stadium, completed in 2019, holds 90,000 people.
✓ The houses built before 1950 need new wiring. (essential: which houses?)

blocks.title: الاسم والوظيفة
blocks.text: لو الوظيفة جاية قبل الاسم على طول (biologist Maria Lopez) أو بعد the لوظيفة عامة فيها ناس كتير، ما تحطش فاصلة. لو الوصف يخص شخص واحد بس (the team's only biologist) يبقى الاسم معلومة إضافية ويتحط بين فاصلتين. وممنوع فاصلة واحدة لوحدها.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1 — closing a dash pair**

Text: Many visitors to Egypt never travel west of the Nile Valley, but those who do are rarely disappointed. The Siwa Oasis—famous for its dates, its olives, and the ruins of an ancient oracle temple ______ lies about 50 kilometers from the Libyan border.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) temple,
B) temple—
C) temple
D) temple;

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: The extra information opened with a dash after “Oasis,” so a comma cannot close it (mismatched pair). Commas also appear inside the list, which is exactly why the writer chose dashes.
B) ✓ Correct: A dash closes the dash pair. Removal test: “The Siwa Oasis lies about 50 kilometers from the Libyan border.” ✓
C) ✗ Wrong: With no closing mark, the reader cannot see where the extra information ends; the sentence becomes confusing.
D) ✗ Wrong: A semicolon needs a complete sentence before it; “The Siwa Oasis—famous for …” has no verb.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — label + name**

Text: Rising water temperatures are a growing concern for fish farmers along the Nile. In 2015, ______ completed a study of how Nile tilapia respond to warmer water, and her results are now used by farms across the region.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) marine biologist Hana Fouad
B) marine biologist, Hana Fouad
C) marine biologist Hana Fouad,
D) marine, biologist Hana Fouad

blocks.text: **Answer: A**

items: A) ✓ Correct: “Marine biologist Hana Fouad” works like a title + name: no comma. The subject goes straight to its verb “completed.”
B) ✗ Wrong: Trap: a comma between a label and the name that follows it. There is also no closing comma, so “Hana Fouad” would be cut off from its sentence.
C) ✗ Wrong: Trap: the lonely comma after the name separates the subject from its verb “completed.”
D) ✗ Wrong: “Marine biologist” is one job label; a comma between the adjective and its noun breaks it.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — which-clause**

Text: Alexandria was home to the most famous library of the ancient world. Today, the city has a modern successor. The Bibliotheca Alexandrina ______ opened in 2002 near the site of the ancient library, has space for millions of books.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) , that
B) which
C) , which
D) that

blocks.text: **Answer: C**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: “That” never takes a comma, and it introduces essential information. Here the clause is closed by a comma after “library,” so it is extra.
B) ✗ Wrong: Trap: the pair is closed after “library” but never opened.
C) ✓ Correct: “Which” introduces extra information, and the opening comma matches the closing comma. Removal: “The Bibliotheca Alexandrina has space for millions of books.” ✓
D) ✗ Wrong: No opening comma, and “that” cannot introduce information that is closed by a comma.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — unique description + name**
Text: Flying was still new and dangerous in the early 1930s, and very few women anywhere had learned to fly. Egypt's first woman pilot ______ earned her license in 1933.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) , Lotfia El Nadi
B) Lotfia El Nadi,
C) , Lotfia El Nadi,
D) Lotfia El Nadi

blocks.text: **Answer: C**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Trap: the pair is opened but never closed, so a single comma splits the name from the verb “earned.”
B) ✗ Wrong: Trap: a closing comma with no opening comma — again a lonely comma between subject and verb.
C) ✓ Correct: “Egypt's first woman pilot” can only be one person, so the name is extra and takes a matching pair of commas. Removal: “Egypt's first woman pilot earned her license in 1933.” ✓
D) ✗ Wrong: Trap: your ear accepts it, but the description already identifies one person, so the name is extra and must be set off.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **The lonely comma:** one comma between a long subject and its verb (“The researchers who studied the samples, concluded …”).
**The mixed pair:** extra information that opens with a dash and closes with a comma, or the reverse.
**The missing partner:** an opening mark with no closing mark (or a closing mark with no opening one).
**The title trap:** “author, Ahmed Khaled” — a comma between a label and a name.
**“, that”:** a comma before “that” is wrong on the test.
**Commas around essential information:** “Students, who study daily, improve fastest” changes the meaning.
**Forgetting the context:** check whether the passage talks about one thing or several before you decide.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Find the skeleton: subject → verb → object. Nothing may separate those parts except a complete matching pair.
Find the extra information and its two edges. Look back (or forward) for the mark that is already there and match it.
Use the removal test for names, appositives and which/who/that clauses.
Label directly before a name = no comma. Unique description + name = pair of commas.
When in doubt between “with commas” and “without commas,” ask: does the sentence before tell me there is only one?

blocks.text: Practice
Ten original Digital SAT-style questions on extra information. Find the edges of the extra information and check that the marks match.

blocks.title: Extra Information — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 10 questions · untimed. Use the removal test, then check that every pair matches.

questions.p: Hatshepsut was not the only woman to rule ancient Egypt, but she was one of the most successful. Hatshepsut, one of the few women to rule ancient Egypt as pharaoh ______ ordered the construction of a great temple at Deir el-Bahari.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The appositive “one of the few women … as pharaoh” opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma. A mixes a comma with a dash, C leaves the pair unclosed, and D puts a semicolon where no independent clause ends.

questions.p: Archaeologists found clay tablets in two different chambers of an ancient building. The tablets ______ were found in the lower chamber are about two hundred years older than the others.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The clause tells us which tablets (those in the lower chamber, not the others), so it is essential: no commas, and “that” is correct. A and B add an opening comma with no closing comma, and C puts a comma between “that” and its verb.

questions.p: Economists disagree about how online shopping has affected small towns in Egypt. In a 2021 report, the economist ______ argued that small online shops had created thousands of new jobs in rural areas.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The passage mentions many economists, so the name tells us which economist: it is essential and takes no commas. B and D leave a single comma that splits the subject from “argued,” and C treats the name as extra, although “the economist” alone does not identify one person.

questions.p: The Delta Science Museum has had just one director since it opened in 1998. The director ______ has overseen three major expansions of the building.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The text says the museum has had only one director, so “the director” already identifies her and the name is extra: it needs a matching pair of commas. B and D use a lonely comma between subject and verb; A treats the name as essential.

questions.p: Some animals are perfectly suited to life in the desert. The camel—valued for centuries by desert travelers for its ability to go many days without water ______ is still used to carry goods in parts of the Sahara.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The extra information opens with a dash after “camel,” so it must close with a dash. B and D mix marks, and C never closes the extra information.

questions.p: Traffic in the city center has grown worse every year. The new metro line (the first in the city to run entirely on solar power ______ is expected to remove thousands of cars from the roads each day.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The extra information opens with a bracket, so it must close with a bracket. A and B mix marks; D leaves the bracket open.

questions.p: The town has two bridges across the river. The bridge ______ is still used by cars, while the newer one, built in 1975, is open only to people on foot.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Because the town has two bridges, “built in 1902” tells us which bridge: it is essential and takes no commas. A treats it as extra; C and D leave a single comma that separates the subject from the verb “is.”

questions.p: Coral reefs in the Red Sea seem to survive heat waves better than reefs in many other seas. A new project to find out why is led by Dr. Laila Mansour ______ has studied Red Sea corals for twenty years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: After a person's name, a who-clause is extra information, so it needs a comma before “who.” A has no comma; B puts a semicolon before a dependent clause; C uses “that” with a comma and uses it for a person.

questions.p: The first test results for the new fertilizer were very encouraging. The final results ______ showed that it worked well only in sandy soil.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: “However” interrupts the clause “The final results showed …,” so it is extra and needs a matching pair of commas. B leaves the pair open; C has no opening comma; D uses a semicolon although “The final results” is not a complete sentence.

questions.p: Hikers who reach the top in the early morning can see the sun rise over the mountains of southern Sinai. Mount Catherine, which rises 2,629 meters above sea level ______ the highest mountain in Egypt.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The which-clause opens with a comma after “Catherine,” so a comma must close it before the verb “is.” A never closes the pair, B mixes a comma with a dash, and D uses a semicolon with no complete sentence before it.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Removal test: if the sentence still works and means the same without the words, they are extra → matching pair (, … , / — … — / ( … )).
Never mix the pair, and never forget the opening or closing mark.
Label directly before a name = no comma; unique description + name = pair of commas.
“which” + commas = extra; “that” + no commas = essential; after a name, “who” takes commas.
Read the context: one thing (extra) or one of several (essential)?
